newsitem.title: USA: U.S. durables drop suggests manufacturing peaked.
newsitem.headline: U.S. durables drop suggests manufacturing peaked.

text.p: The sharpest decline in orders for U.S. durable goods in more than a year could mean a rebound in manufacturing has peaked, economists said.
"This is a number the markets will embrace as a sign activity in the manufacturing sector is slowing," said Kevin Flanagan, vice president and an economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

Orders for durable goods in August fell 3.1 percent, compared with a downwardly revised 1.4 percent jump in July, the Commerce Department said. Excluding defense, orders fell 3.5 percent for the data's biggest drop since July 1993.
Economists in a Reuters survey forecast durable goods fell 0.1 percent in August, and down 0.7 percent without defense components. Individual forecasts ranged from down 1.0 percent to up 2.0 percent.

Economists warned the data is one of the most volatile of closely-watched statistics. The number appears to underpin the Federal Reserve's decision to leave short-term rates untouched earlier this week, however.
"It's only one month's worth of data and it's the first real meaningful decline we've had in a while, so you don't want to rush to any conclusions," Flanagan said.
"But given the fact that the Fed did not tighten earlier this week, the market will take comfort in the notion that the Fed sees more slowing than some numbers portend," he added.

Tim McGee, chief economist at Tokai Bank Ltd, also said the data confirm Chairman Alan Greenspan's view of a slowing economy, adding that a rate hike on Tuesday might have only necessitated a rate cut next year.
The U.S. Treasury 30-year bond popped up almost 1/2 point after the release to yield 6.89 percent at 0930 EDT/1330 GMT.
A 7.9-percent decline in transportation equipment surprised economists, many of whom expected aircraft orders at Boeing Co to beef up the number after months of weakness.

"We're suprised that transportation is still on the weak side," Flanagan said. "There were orders that apparently booked a month or so ago and we've yet to see them. If they are included and you're still down 7.9 percent that would be very, very surprising."
Transportation equipment for July was revised downward to post a 1.6 percent decline from a 0.4 percent slide originally. The component dropped 1.3 percent in June.

Despite chances for a rebound in September, economists said the decline is certain to be a drag on third-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP). That, in turn, provides another pat on the central bank's back, said Irwin Kellner, chief economist at Chase Regional Bank.
"If you take (out) transportation, (orders) were down (1.6 percent)," Kellner said. "It's pretty clear this was a weak figure even allowing for the volatility."

Cary Leahey, senior financial market economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc, also said the trend of stronger growth has shifted. He said a third-quarter GDP number below 2.0 percent, perhaps as low as 1.5 percent, is likely.
For all the apparent weakness, some economists noted shipments continue to flow out and inventories should remain on the leaner side.

"It's not as if you're building a case of a problem for manufacturing in the future," Flanagan said. "What you could be seeing here is just a volatile series that hasn't had a significant decline in a while showing up."
